correctness.rationale: A proper clique-bouquet coloring uses one exclusive hub color and distinct colors within each clique; hence all nonhub vertices automatically have pairwise distinct neighborhood colors. The hub permits exactly positive odd multiplicities among the selected peripheral colors. The signed parity projector on the polynomial product of elementary symmetric functions selects exactly these labelings and yields the stated binomial sum with the correct factorial, hub and palette factors. When t is odd the clique lower bound is attained; when t is even each selected color occurs at most t-1 times and k is even, forcing the displayed bound. An odd column-degree assignment followed by binary-matrix row-degree balancing attains the bound. A current standalone checker independently tests 151311 center-normalized assignments across 138 comparisons and 570 uniform constructions; these computations are corroboration, not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The initiating arXiv:2401.11653 and the primary arXiv:2410.02336 give definition, broad bounds and claw-free results, not a full counting polynomial on arbitrary clique bouquets. The claw-free theorem may imply the two-blade scalar corollary, which is not claimed as new on its own. Arxiv:2602.03259 treats cycle-based joins and gluing. A newer arXiv:2610.01441 abstract announces a broad block-graph optimal-coloring algorithm, but not an all-palette enumerator; its unavailable full text remains a specific residual risk. The final polynomial records every named-palette strong-odd coloring for every nonuniform blade-size vector, not merely the known minimum.

value.rationale: The clique bouquet is the natural star-of-cliques block-graph operation, and strong-odd feasibility introduces a nonlocal hub parity condition despite all noncentral neighborhood constraints being automatic. The result counts the entire feasible coloring space and exposes the exact odd/even blade-number transition in uniform bouquets. The parity projector and balancing argument explain a structural incidence obstruction, giving meaningful information not implied by a single optimum or a routine graph-coloring substitution.
